chunks.text: 3 Methods Conventional adapters for pretrained models typically rely on low-rank linear updates or generic MLPs. While effective, these mechanisms introduce largely unstructured nonlinear transformations. We instead consider frozen-backbone adaptation under limited data, where the geometry of pretrained representations should be preserved while enabling controlled feature reshaping. Our objective is to design a compact nonlinear adapter that introduces structured spectral lifting, maintains bounded activations, and remains computationally lightweight. Let ℱ ϕ \mathcal{F}_{\phi} denote a pretrained backbone with parameters ϕ \phi . Given downstream data 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\} , we operate in the frozen regime where ϕ \phi remains fixed and only an adaptation module and task-specific head are optimized. We seek a structured nonlinear transformation that modulates intermediate features without disrupting pretrained representation geometry. We refer to this module as the Quantum-Inspired Nonlinear Adapter (QINA) . Inspired by quantum information theory [ Nielsen and Chuang(2010) ] , where high-dimensional systems remain stable through structured operators and constrained state evolution [ Lorenz and Barrett(2021) ] , QINA acts on latent features while preserving pretrained backbones. Although the design is inspired by trigonometric phase encodings used in quantum circuit formulations, it is implemented entirely as a differentiable real-valued transformation on classical hardware. Figure 1 shows the proposed QINA block and how it can be integrated into the CNN and transformer backbones. Figure 1 : Structured spectral adaptation via QINA in frozen backbones. Left: Internal architecture of the QINA module, consisting of linear encoding, trigonometric lifting, linear decoding, and bounded nonlinearity.

Middle: In residual CNN blocks, QINA operates within the residual branch on intermediate feature maps, producing a bounded correction that is added to the shortcut connection while keeping the backbone parameters frozen. Right: In Transformer encoder layers, QINA is inserted before MHA in the first residual block. 3.1 QINA Formulation Let X ∈ ℝ H × W × C X\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} denote a feature tensor from an intermediate backbone layer. Flattening spatial dimensions yields X flat ∈ ℝ C × N X_{\text{flat}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N} with N = H × W N=H\times W . QINA performs structured trigonometric lifting or phase encoding followed by bounded nonlinear aggregation: Linear Projection P = W enc ​ X flat + b enc ∈ ℝ d × N , P=W_{\text{enc}}X_{\text{flat}}+b_{\text{enc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, (1) Trigonometric Lifting A = sin ⁡ ( P ) + cos ⁡ ( P ) ∈ ℝ d × N , A=\sin(P)+\cos(P)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, (2) Linear Decoding S = W dec ​ A + b dec ∈ ℝ C × N , S=W_{\text{dec}}A+b_{\text{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times N}, (3) Bounded Nonlinearity R = tanh ⁡ ( S ) , R=\tanh(S), (4) where W enc ∈ ℝ d × C W_{\text{enc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times C} , b enc ∈ ℝ d b_{\text{enc}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , W dec ∈ ℝ C × d W_{\text{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d} , and b dec ∈ ℝ C b_{\text{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} are learnable parameters and d d denotes the projection dimension. The phase mapping in Equation 2 can be interpreted as a learnable Fourier-type feature expansion. Unlike random Fourier features, projection frequencies and decoding weights are optimized jointly with the downstream objective. This structure introduces oscillatory basis functions capable of representing higher-frequency components that may not be efficiently captured by linear adapters. The tanh \tanh activation bounds the adapter output, providing a functional analogy to the bounded expectation-value outputs in PQCs.

QINA does not implement quantum states, observables, entanglement, or a quantum algorithm; it is a trigonometric adapter motivated by PQC functional forms. Without the final nonlinearity, the module reduces to a shallow linear decoding of learned trigonometric features. The bounded activation limits output magnitude and derivative amplification, providing controlled feature modulation under frozen-backbone adaptation. Thus, QINA acts as a structured spectral adapter rather than a generic MLP. 3.2 Approximation Perspective QINA can be viewed as a learnable trigonometric feature expansion. We provide a simple approximation argument to clarify its expressive capacity. Proposition 1 . Let f : ℝ C → ℝ f:\mathbb{R}^{C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous function with bounded spectral support. For any ε > 0 \varepsilon>0 , there exists a projection dimension d d and parameters ( W enc , W dec ) (W_{\mathrm{enc}},W_{\mathrm{dec}}) such that a QINA module approximates f f uniformly on compact subsets of ℝ C \mathbb{R}^{C} with error at most ε \varepsilon . Proof Sketch. By Fourier approximation, such functions admit finite trigonometric expansions: f ⁡ ( x ) ≈ ∑ k = 1 d ( a k ​ cos ⁡ ( ω k ⊤ ​ x ) + b k ​ sin ⁡ ( ω k ⊤ ​ x ) ) . f(x)\approx\sum_{k=1}^{d}\left(a_{k}\cos(\omega_{k}^{\top}x)+b_{k}\sin(\omega_{k}^{\top}x)\right). (5) Choosing rows of W enc W_{\mathrm{enc}} as frequencies ω k \omega_{k} and letting W dec W_{\mathrm{dec}} implement the linear combination recovers this expansion. The applied tanh \tanh preserves universal approximation on compact domains while enforcing bounded output geometry. ∎ Corollary 1 . Increasing the projection dimension reduces approximation error for functions with higher spectral complexity at fixed backbone representations. This perspective explains the empirical observation that larger d d improves performance in low-data regimes: increasing d d increases effective spectral resolution without modifying the frozen backbone.

(6) Using the chain rule, the Jacobian satisfies ∇ Φ ​ ( x ) = diag ⁡ ( 1 − tanh 2 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) ) ​ W dec ​ diag ​ ( cos ⁡ ( W enc ​ x ) − sin ⁡ ( W enc ​ x ) ) ​ W enc . \nabla\Phi(x)=\mathrm{diag}\!\left(1-\tanh^{2}(\cdot)\right)\,W_{\mathrm{dec}}\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\cos(W_{\mathrm{enc}}x)-\sin(W_{\mathrm{enc}}x)\right)\,W_{\mathrm{enc}}. (7) Since | 1 − tanh 2 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) | ≤ 1 |1-\tanh^{2}(\cdot)|\leq 1 and | cos ⁡ ( u ) − sin ⁡ ( u ) | ≤ 2 |\cos(u)-\sin(u)|\leq\sqrt{2} , QINA is globally Lipschitz continuous with an input-independent but parameter-dependent bound: ‖ ∇ Φ ​ ( x ) ‖ 2 ≤ 2 ​ ‖ W dec ‖ 2 ​ ‖ W enc ‖ 2 . \|\nabla\Phi(x)\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{2}\,\|W_{\mathrm{dec}}\|_{2}\|W_{\mathrm{enc}}\|_{2}. (8) Thus, the nonlinearities provide bounded input response, while the Lipschitz constant remains proportional to the learned spectral norms of W enc W_{\mathrm{enc}} and W dec W_{\mathrm{dec}} . We do not impose explicit spectral-norm constraints, and this should not be seen as a norm-independent stability guarantee. Connection to Kernel Feature Maps. Random Fourier features approximate shift-invariant kernels using fixed sampled frequencies. QINA can be interpreted as a learnable analogue in which projection frequencies are optimized jointly with the downstream task. This induces a data-dependent spectral feature map rather than a fixed random embedding. Relation to MLP Adapters. Standard MLPs are universal approximators. QINA does not replace this result; instead, it restricts the hypothesis class to structured trigonometric expansions followed by bounded nonlinear aggregation. Compared to MLP adapters, this imposes an explicit spectral bias, improving stability and generalization when data is limited and the backbone is frozen.

3.3 Integration into Vision Backbones CNN Backbones. In convolutional networks, QINA is inserted into the residual bottleneck structure, preserving residual learning behavior and allowing the residual correction branch to compensate if the nonlinear adapter introduces noise or limited expressivity. The adapter operates on intermediate feature maps and returns a correction of matching dimensionality, allowing the network to retain pretrained representations while enabling structured nonlinear modulation. Because the backbone remains frozen, insertion does not disrupt pretrained filters but provides a controlled residual adjustment. Vision Transformers. In the transformer architecture, adapters are inserted before the multi-head attention (MHA) module within the first residual encoder block to better align with the attention mechanism. Empirical evaluation showed that placing the adapter after the MHA module, where it operates directly on the token embeddings, led to inferior performance. 4 Experiments We empirically evaluate whether a compact, structured nonlinear adapter, inserted into a pretrained backbone, improves frozen-backbone adaptation under low-data and domain-shift settings. All experiments are designed to isolate representational effects from parameter count and architectural confounders. 4.1 Training Protocol Backbones. For classification, we use pretrained ResNet-18 [ He et al.(2016)He, Zhang, Ren, and Sun ] , Xception [ Fran(2017) ] , and ViT-Tiny [ Dosovitskiy et al.(2021)Dosovitskiy, Beyer, Kolesnikov, Weissenborn, Zhai, Unterthiner, Dehghani, Minderer, Heigold, Gelly, et al. , Touvron et al.(2021)Touvron, Cord, Douze, Massa, Sablayrolles, and Jégou ] . ResNet-18 is used within DeepLabv3+ [ Chen et al.(2018)Chen, Zhu, Papandreou, Schroff, and Adam ] for segmentation. All backbones are pretrained on ImageNet using supervised objectives. Frozen Adaptation. In the primary setting, all backbone parameters remain frozen.

Only the inserted adapter and task-specific head are optimized. This isolates the effect of representation reshaping without modifying pretrained filters. Full Fine-Tuning. For comparison, we also evaluate end-to-end fine-tuning, updating all backbone parameters. This assesses whether adapter advantages persist when representation geometry is allowed to change. Low-Data Regimes. To evaluate representational efficiency, we simulate stratified labeling budgets of { 5 , 10 , 20 , 50 , 100 , 200 , 500 } \{5,10,20,50,100,200,500\} samples. A fixed 20% held-out validation split is selected before subsampling and reused only for evaluation across all experiments. All budgeted training sets are drawn exclusively from the remaining 80% of the data. All configurations follow the same fixed-step training protocol. Each configuration is repeated with five random seeds, resulting in 35 models per backbone per dataset. Optimization Setting. We use Adam with an initial learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Batch size is 32 for classification and 8 for segmentation. Standard geometric and photometric augmentations (horizontal flip, rotation, translation, contrast/brightness jitter, Gaussian noise) are applied during training. To ensure fair comparison across budgets, we normalize training by fixing the total number of optimization steps to 500 per experiment. The number of epochs is then adjusted according to dataset size, batch size, and optimization steps, and bounded within [10,100] to prevent under- or overfitting. 4.2 Datasets and Tasks We evaluate the adapters across nine dataset-task settings from natural and medical imaging. Frozen pretrained backbone with task-specific linear head only. MLP Adapter. A parameter-matched MLP block inserted at the same location as QINA. We evaluate linear, ReLU, and tanh activations instead of phase encoding. Fourier Features. A sinusoidal embedding ϕ ⁡ ( x ) = sin ⁡ ( W ​ x ) \phi(x)=\sin(Wx) with randomly sampled frequencies ( W ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) W\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) ). This baseline controls for gains arising from adding trigonometric basis functions without learnable spectral structure.

QINA Block. Learnable trigonometric projection with learned frequencies followed by bounded nonlinear aggregation. Adapters are inserted at all-, low-, mid-, and high-level feature layers. Projection dimension d d varies from 16 to 512 to analyze spectral capacity scaling and the impact of adapter dimensionality. LoRA Block. This configuration is selected based on the ablation study in Section 5.4 , where it provides a strong balance between accuracy and computational complexity. For clarity of presentation, we visualize the main results in plots; detailed numerical results and complexity comparisons are provided in Appendix . 5.1 Natural Image Classification We first evaluate on STL-10 using different pretrained classification backbones.

Figure 3 summarizes model performance across training budgets. Across all budgets and architectures, inserting QINA consistently improves validation accuracy compared to the baselines. The improvement is particularly pronounced for ViT-Tiny at moderate-to-high budgets. Notably, the performance gap between QINA and the identity baseline (frozen backbone with no adapter) remains substantial even as the number of labeled samples increases. These results suggest that, under frozen-backbone training, performance is primarily representation-limited rather than head-capacity-limited. The linear head largely exploits the existing feature geometry, whereas QINA introduces a structured nonlinear transformation that better aligns pretrained features with the downstream label structure. Importantly, the consistent superiority of QINA over both fixed Fourier expansions and generic MLP adapters suggests that performance gains cannot be attributed solely to increased nonlinear capacity. Instead, the structured spectral parameterization appears to provide a more effective mechanism for reshaping pretrained representations under frozen constraints. Figure 3 : Validation performance on STL-10 under frozen-backbone training across different classification backbones and training budgets. QINA consistently improves performance across models and budgets. 5.2 Medical Image Classification We next evaluate on medical classification datasets using pretrained CNN backbones. Results are shown in Figure 4 . Again, QINA consistently improves performance across datasets and budgets. The relative gain is more pronounced for ResNet-18, particularly in lower-budget regimes. As in the natural-image setting, the identity baseline exhibits a clear performance gap compared to QINA. The performance ranking across datasets and models remains stable as the training budget increases.

This indicates that additional data improves decision boundary estimation but does not fundamentally alter which representation is most suitable. In other words, the dominant factor in frozen adaptation is representation alignment rather than classifier capacity or budget. Figure 4 : Validation performance on medical classification datasets under frozen-backbone training across different CNN backbones and training budgets. QINA consistently improves performance across models, datasets, and budgets. Domain Shift Analysis. We further analyze the role of domain shift. When pretrained models trained on natural images are applied to STL-10, semantic hierarchies and image statistics remain reasonably aligned with pretraining. In this regime, specific backbone layers exhibit clear abstraction advantages. However, medical datasets differ substantially from natural images in image statistics (grayscale structure, modality-specific artifacts, low texture diversity) and semantic organization. Under such domain shift, no single backbone layer is strongly aligned with the downstream task. Early layers capture generic edges and noise patterns, while late layers encode high-level natural-image semantics that transfer weakly. Middle layers provide partial but imperfect alignment. In this setting, improvements from QINA arise from nonlinear mixing and feature reshaping rather than intrinsic backbone quality. Additional labeled data refines the classifier but does not introduce missing invariances or modality-specific structure. For further interpretation, we fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet on FETAL ultrasound data and subsequently freeze this adapted backbone for classification on BUSI. Although the tasks differ, the imaging modality is shared. As shown in Figure 5 , freezing the modality-adapted backbone yields a substantial performance improvement compared to freezing the original ImageNet backbone.

After modality alignment, representation-level differences across layers re-emerge. Higher layers regain abstraction advantage, and the behavior becomes more similar to the STL-10 setting. This supports the interpretation that representation alignment, rather than head capacity, was the primary bottleneck under strong domain shift. Figure 5 : BUSI classification performance using a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet versus a frozen modality-adapted ResNet fine-tuned on FETAL ultrasound data. Although the tasks differ, modality alignment significantly improves downstream performance under freezing. 5.3 Medical Image Segmentation To verify that the observed behavior is not specific to classification, we evaluate QINA within DeepLabv3+ segmentation pipelines while modifying only the pretrained backbone representation. As shown in Figure 6 , QINA improves validation performance across most budgets and datasets. Gains are particularly visible for Kvasir and Cardiac datasets at moderate-to-high budgets. The consistent gap relative to the identity baseline and MLP adapters indicates that structured nonlinear adaptation at the backbone level provides a more effective representation reshaping mechanism that benefits both classification and dense prediction tasks. These findings suggest that QINA enhances representational alignment rather than merely improving classifier expressivity. Figure 6 : Validation performance (foreground Dice) on medical segmentation datasets using DeepLabv3+ with a frozen pretrained encoder. Consistent improvements across budgets suggest that structured nonlinear adaptation benefits dense prediction tasks. 5.4 Ablation Study We conduct controlled ablations on STL-10 to isolate three design factors: where adaptation is applied (placement), how much spectral capacity is provided (projection dimension), and whether the benefit is specific to frozen representations (full fine-tuning).

Figure 7 summarizes these experiments; complementary ablations are provided in Appendix . Placement. Inserting QINA at higher layers consistently yields the strongest performance, followed by mid-layer and lower-layer placements. In contrast, distributing adapters across all layers with a matched total parameter budget is less effective, likely due to the introduction of low-dimensional bottlenecks. These results suggest that, under a frozen-backbone setting, adapting higher-level abstract representations with greater capacity is more beneficial than modifying early, edge-level features. Dimension. Increasing the hidden dimension d d improves performance across budgets. The QINA block can be interpreted as a learnable Fourier-type feature expansion of dimension d d . Larger d d increases effective feature rank and reduces approximation error of the nonlinear mapping, thereby enhancing representational capacity particularly in low-data regimes. However, computational cost also increases. We select d = 128 d=128 as a balanced trade-off between accuracy and complexity across budgets. Fine-tuning. When the backbone is unfrozen and trained end-to-end, the performance gap between QINA and baselines diminishes substantially. In this regime, optimization and inductive bias dominate, and data is no longer the bottleneck; the backbone adapts to the downstream task, reshaping the entire feature hierarchy. Fine-tuning erases layer-choice bias, and representational differences introduced by adapter placement become less critical. This observation reinforces the primary conclusion of our study: QINA is particularly effective in frozen-backbone or low-data regimes where representation alignment is constrained. Under full fine-tuning with sufficient data, optimization can compensate for representational misalignment, reducing the relative benefit of lightweight adapters.

Figure 7 : Ablations on STL-10 evaluating QINA placement (left), hidden dimension (middle), and full fine-tuning (right). Higher-layer insertion and larger hidden dimension improve accuracy in the frozen regime, whereas end-to-end fine-tuning reduces adapter-specific gains. 5.5 Representation Analysis QINA’s trigonometric lifting introduces periodic basis functions that enable the adapter to represent higher-frequency components within the frozen backbone. Increasing the projection dimension d d expands the adapter’s spectral resolution while leaving the backbone unchanged, providing a structured mechanism for reshaping feature geometry under frozen transfer. To examine the resulting representations, we analyze feature statistics of a ResNet-18 backbone on STL-10 using a representative labeled budget of 500 training samples. Similar qualitative trends were observed across other labeling budgets. We evaluate three complementary metrics on the validation representations from the inserted blocks: Fisher Discriminant Ratio (FDR), which measures class separability; Effective Rank (ER) [ Roy and Vetterli(2007) ] , which characterizes the compactness of feature covariance; and Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) [ Kornblith et al.(2019)Kornblith, Norouzi, Lee, and Hinton ] , which quantifies similarity between adapted and baseline representations. Results are shown in Figure 8 . Compared to identity, MLP, and Fourier baselines, QINA features achieve the highest FDR while exhibiting lower ER and lower CKA relative to the alternative blocks. Higher FDR indicates improved class separation, while reduced ER suggests more compact feature utilization. Lower CKA indicates that the adapter introduces a nontrivial transformation of the representation geometry rather than preserving the original backbone structure.

Together, these observations suggest that QINA reshapes frozen feature representations toward more discriminative and compact embeddings while maintaining a low parameter footprint. This behavior is consistent with the role of structured trigonometric lifting in compensating for the low-frequency bias of frozen convolutional representations. Higher-layer insertion and larger hidden dimension improve accuracy in the frozen regime, whereas end-to-end fine-tuning reduces adapter-specific gains. 6 Conclusion We investigated frozen-backbone adaptation through the lens of representation alignment and structured nonlinear transformation. Rather than redesigning full architectures or pursuing quantum computational speedup, we introduced a compact quantum-inspired nonlinear adapter (QINA) that performs learnable trigonometric feature lifting followed by bounded nonlinear aggregation.

QINA introduces three key properties: structured oscillatory basis functions applied within intermediate feature spaces, bounded smooth nonlinearities with a Lipschitz bound governed by the learned weight norms, and a lightweight residual formulation that preserves pretrained representation geometry. Together, these characteristics provide an inductive bias that complements frozen pretrained backbones without disrupting their hierarchical structure. Across classification and segmentation tasks in natural and medical imaging, we observed three consistent findings. First, in frozen regimes, performance is primarily representation-limited rather than classifier-limited. Second, nonlinear lifting improves adaptation under low-data and domain-shift settings. Third, and most importantly, across the evaluated frozen-backbone settings, structured trigonometric lifting with learnable frequencies consistently outperforms both fixed Fourier embeddings and parameter-matched baseline adapters. This indicates that performance gains arise not merely from increased nonlinear capacity, but from the imposed spectral structure and controlled output geometry. Our findings suggest that adapter effectiveness depends on representational alignment, placement, and geometric constraints. While quantum-inspired formulations motivate the trigonometric design, the proposed module operates entirely within standard deep learning frameworks and remains computationally efficient. Overall, this work highlights the importance of structured nonlinear adapters for frozen transfer learning and provides a controlled empirical and theoretical analysis of spectral feature lifting within modern vision backbones. Appendix C QINA Component Ablations To isolate the contributions of QINA’s trigonometric encoding and bounded output nonlinearity, we evaluate alternative choices on STL-10 using ResNet-18 while keeping the backbone, adapter placement, hidden dimension, training budgets, and optimization protocol fixed. As shown in the left panel of Figure 9 , sine-only, cosine-only, and combined sine–cosine encodings achieve similar performance across training budgets. This behavior is expected because the three parameterizations are closely related by phase shifts and scaling: cos ⁡ ( P ) = sin ⁡ ( P + π / 2 ) \cos(P)=\sin(P+\pi/2) and sin ⁡ ( P ) + cos ⁡ ( P ) = 2 ​ sin ⁡ ( P + π / 4 ) \sin(P)+\cos(P)=\sqrt{2}\sin(P+\pi/4) . Since the phase projection contains a learnable bias and is followed by a learned decoder, much of these differences can be absorbed during optimization. The combined sine–cosine encoding nevertheless provides a small empirical advantage and is therefore used in QINA. The right panel evaluates the final bounded nonlinearity by replacing tanh \tanh with a linear output. Both variants perform similarly, although tanh \tanh provides a small improvement across the evaluated budgets. This suggests that the main benefit does not depend critically on the output nonlinearity, while the bounded tanh \tanh transformation provides a modest empirical advantage and retains the bounded-output property used in the QINA formulation.
